title: Time's Answer to Arjuna
subtitle: Vyasa consoles the grieving archer, and Parikshit is enthroned
story:
When the news reached him, Arjuna went to Dwaraka alone.

Krishna and Balarama had left the world, and their city was a city of the dead. Arjuna performed the last rites for the two brothers and for all the slain. The eight queens of Krishna, Rukmini at their head, embraced the body of their lord and entered the funeral fire; Revati, holding the body of Rama, entered the blazing pile, and the fire, the verses say, was cool to her, happy in her contact with her lord. Hearing this, Ugrasena and Vasudeva, with Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames. Arjuna performed their rites too, then made the whole city rise and leave. He took Vajra, the young prince of the Yadus, and led the thousands of Krishna's wives and all the people of Dwaraka slowly away with tenderness and care.

Behind them, the Sudharman palace and the Parijata tree, which Krishna had brought down to earth, rose and went back to heaven. On the same day Hari left the earth, the dark-bodied Kali age descended. And the ocean rose and submerged all of Dwaraka, save one small temple of the Yadu deity, which the sea has never washed away; there, they say, Kesava still abides, and whoever visits it is freed from sins.

Arjuna halted the great company in the Panchanada country, a rich and fertile land. But the robbers of the region saw a single warrior in charge of so many widowed women and so much treasure, and their greed woke. They gathered the lawless Abhiras to them. "Here is Arjuna," they said, "rich, and proud of slaying Bhishma and Drona and Karna. He does not know the prowess of simple villagers. Up! Take your staves! Why should we not lift our arms?" And they rushed at the people with cudgels and clods of earth.

Arjuna faced them. "Retire, wretches," he said, "unless you wish to die." They paid him no heed; they seized the treasure and the women. Arjuna reached for his heavenly bow, Gandiva — and it would not brace. The string stayed slack in his hands, however he strained. The incantations of the superhuman weapons would not come back to his memory. He loosed arrows as best he could, and they merely scratched skin; even the shafts Agni had given him were themselves destroyed. He beat at the bandits with the horn of his bow, and they laughed. And in the sight of Arjuna, the barbarians carried off the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes and went their way.

Then the greatest archer of the age broke down. "Alas, alas!" he wept. "I am deserted by my lord!" And in that instant Gandiva and the heavenly weapons, his chariot and his horses, perished before his eyes. "Resistless are the decrees of fate," he said, "who gave feebleness to me and victory to the base. These arms are mine; this fist is mine; I am Arjuna. But without that righteous aid all of it is pithless — and without him I am overcome by peasants."

He went on to Mathura and installed the young Yadava prince Vajra as its king. And there, in a wood, he found the sage Vyasa and prostrated himself at his feet. Vyasa looked at him for a long time. "How is it, Arjuna," he asked, "that I see you shorn of your lustre? Have you been beaten by your inferiors in battle?"

Arjuna sighed deeply and told him everything. "Hari, who was our strength, our heroism, our very brightness, has left us," he said. "Without him we are as weak as straw. Gandiva, famed through the three worlds, is foiled by the sticks of peasants; the household of Krishna is carried off by thieves with cudgels. It is not that my lustre is gone — it is a wonder that I live."

Vyasa's answer was gentle, and it was absolute. "Think no more of your disgrace, my son," he said. "Know that time subjects all beings to the same vicissitudes. Rivers, seas, mountains, gods, men, trees, insects — all are created by time and destroyed by time. Krishna came down to lift the burden of the earth; that object is accomplished. All the kings are slain, the Vrishni race is destroyed; nothing remained for him to do, and so the lord has departed, his ends fulfilled. At creation he creates, in duration he preserves, at the end he destroys. Your defeat by miserable thieves was as much his work as your victories over Bhishma and Karna. It is only the sport of the universal Hari."

Then Vyasa told him a story. Once, a brahman named Ashtavakra — a great ascetic, crooked in eight places — stood in water for years, meditating. After the Asuras were overthrown, the nymphs of heaven passed that way to a festival on Mount Meru; seeing the sage, they praised him. "Ask what you wish," he said. Some asked for the best of husbands, a sovereign of the Brahmans. "So be it," he said, and rose from the water — and when the nymphs saw how crooked his body was, they laughed. The sage cursed them: "You shall have the first of males for your husband, but because you laughed at my deformity, you shall afterwards fall into the hands of thieves." They begged his pardon, and he softened: in time, he said, they would return to the sphere of the gods.

"It is because of that curse," Vyasa said, "that the wives of Kesava have now fallen into the hands of the barbarians. Do not grieve for it. All this destruction was effected by the lord of all — and your end, too, is near, since he has withdrawn your strength and your splendour. Death is the doom of everyone born; fall is the end of exaltation; union ends in separation; growth tends to decay. Knowing this, wise men are touched by neither grief nor joy. Relinquish everything, and repair to the holy forest. Go and tell Yudhishthira that tomorrow, with his brothers, he must tread the path of heroes."

Arjuna went back and told his brothers all that he had seen and heard. And the sons of Pandu placed Parikshit on the throne, and went to the forest.
reflection: Vyasa's consolation rests on a single recognition: Krishna's coming and going alike were the working of time, which gives and takes away without partiality. The Ashtavakra story makes the point gently — even heavenly nymphs were promised to thieves by an old curse — so that Arjuna's defeat loses its sting: it was never his to keep, and never his loss alone.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana gives a somewhat different account of Dwaraka's end and the deaths of the elders; this story follows the Vishnu Purana, as cited in the evidence pack.
content_note: Contains the funeral-pyre deaths of Krishna's queens and family elders after his death, and an attack by robbers; may warrant parental awareness for younger readers.
next_story_tease: The Pandavas turned their backs on the throne and took the road to the forest — and to Samanta-panchaka.
hero_scene: In a forest hermitage, the sage Vyasa raises a hand as he speaks to the dejected Arjuna, who lies prostrate before him with the great bow Gandiva lying slack beside him on the ground.
